rationale: B wins because it keeps its hands cleaner: it turns the same facts into pitchable questions instead of declaring answers Patagonia has not proved. A's top angle says "no major apparel brand has attempted" and its counterposition says the program is "designed to shorten its own sales pipeline"; both are good instincts wearing borrowed certainty. B's "Patagonia has resold 500,000 used items — and won't say what resale is worth to it" is the best spine here: hard number, disclosure gap, and a reporter-shaped assignment.
gaps_in_A: "no major apparel brand has attempted" and "no comparable US apparel brand has matched" are unsupported category claims. That needs a market scan, not confidence font.
"designed to shorten its own sales pipeline" asserts intent and economic effect Patagonia did not give you. Ask whether repairs reduce new purchases; don't state it as design.
"no publicly traded apparel company could defend to shareholders" is too sweeping. It may be the thesis, but it needs an analyst or public-company operator before it becomes a pitchable line.
"The free jacket repair" smuggles in a product-specific customer scene. The update says any Patagonia item and gives no customer anecdote.
gaps_in_B: "Only a company with no shareholders to please could give repairs away" is punchy, but overclean. Privately held companies still have owners; the line needs softening or proof.
"triages it into free/at-cost/resale" invents an operational link between repairs and resale that the update does not establish.
"Most apparel reverse logistics is returns processing" is useful context, but it is unsourced context. Put a source behind it or frame it as the reporter's question.

"Free repairs at every store cut against how apparel retail makes money" and "Only a company with no shareholders to please could give repairs away" partially overlap. The business-model angle and ownership-mechanism angle need a sharper wall between them.
